In the context of a procedure under Article 60 GDPR, the Irish DPC reprimanded Microsoft Operations Ireland Limited for violations of Article 12(4) GDPR and Article 17 GDPR.

The Danish supervisory authority opened a supervision case on 29 August 2023 into the National Audit Office's legal basis for obtaining personal data during its audits, and how it complies with data minimisation. The authority found that the audit office has a legal basis under Article 6(1)(e) GDPR read with section 12(1) of the Rigsrevisorloven, and that it obtains no more data than necessary. The case was closed with no criticism and no infringement found. The authority noted with approval that the audit office had introduced a requirement to document its need for personal data.

Romania's data protection authority finished an investigation into Rompetrol Downstream SRL in October 2023. The investigation was opened after the company sent several personal data breach notifications between July 2021 and February 2022. Employees had accessed customer data in the company's software without authorisation and unlawfully disclosed it so that loans could be obtained from non-bank financial companies in the customers' names. The authority found a breach of Article 32 GDPR and imposed a contravention fine of 546,073 lei, stated as equivalent to EUR 110,000.

The Belgian DPA reprimanded a controller, an online booking platform, for failing to comply with Article 12(3) GDPR and because Article 6(1)(f) GDPR was not a valid legal basis to publish personal data of health professionals on the platform.

A complainant said that a leasing company's property advertisement photo showed his car with a legible licence plate, and that his access request did not result in the photo being provided. The Authority found that the company breached the data minimisation principle (Art. 5(1)(c)) and the right of access (Art. 15(1)). It imposed two fines of EUR 10,000 each, EUR 20,000 in total. In setting them it took into account that the photo was deleted promptly after the erasure request and that only the complainant was affected.

The French DPA found that two French Ministries had breached Article 5(1)(b) GDPR. The Ministries had used the email addresses of 2,346,303 public servants to share a video promoting the pension reform - against the original purposes of the data processing, limited to administrative communications to employees.

The Danish DPA examined the Agency for Digital Government's use of JavaScript to display the MitID login client, which citizens need enabled in their browsers. It opened the case on its own initiative after a citizen complaint that JavaScript is insecure. The Agency had a general risk assessment of MitID but had not specifically assessed the risks JavaScript poses to data subjects. The DPA issued a reprimand (kritik) for breaching Articles 5(2) with 5(1)(f) and 24(1) with 32(1), and expects a specific assessment of JavaScript risks.

The Danish supervisory authority examined the Danish Agency for Digitalisation's operation of the digital driving licence app after a citizen's complaint. It found that by storing a copy of the driving licence register data for all about 3.96 million valid licence holders, although only about 1.7 million use the app, the agency breached the data minimisation principle. It issued a reprimand and ordered the agency to stop storing and processing data from the register on people who have not actively joined the digital licence, within 4 weeks.
The Hellenic DPA fined a controller €60,000 for unauthorised disclosure of personal data to a data subject's wife.

After a complaint, IMY examined an investment firm, Indecap AB, which on 20 January 2021 mistakenly emailed a customer-data file to about 2,800 unauthorised recipients. The file held unencrypted personal data, including personal identity numbers and financial data, on about 52,000 customers, because a staff member attached an Excel working file instead of the PDF report. IMY found that the company had not taken adequate technical and organisational measures under Article 32(1) GDPR, and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 500,000.

A municipal employee (head of the technical service) complained that the Mayor's decision naming her, together with a criminal complaint against her and a preliminary inquiry, was published in full on the Diavgeia transparency portal. Her personal data also appeared in a Financial Committee invitation and decision, and her erasure request was refused. The Authority found unlawful publication of the Mayor's decision (Art. 5(1)(a), 6(1)(c)) and fined the municipality EUR 2,000. It reprimanded the municipality for a second Mayor's decision, found a data minimisation breach (Art. 5(1)(c)) for the Financial Committee decision and invitation (EUR 1,000), and found an Art. 17(1) erasure breach (EUR 2,000). It ordered deletion and re-publication of the documents and recommended that the legislator set criteria for what personal data is published online.

A prosecutor had a residence information block (Auskunftssperre) in the central register of residents. An employee of the municipality queried her registered main residence and passed it to a private detective agency without notifying her or giving her a chance to respond. The authority upheld the complaint and found that the municipality infringed the complainant's right to secrecy by breaching the notification duty in § 18(5) of the Austrian Registration Act. No fine or order is stated in the text.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation at OTP Bank Romania SA in October 2023, started by a complaint. The bank had not applied sufficient security measures, and a complainant's personal data was sent by e-mail to another person. The bank also failed to notify the authority of this security incident. It was fined RON 14,889.3 (about EUR 3,000) under Article 32 and given a warning under Article 33, with corrective orders on security measures and breach handling.

A data subject asked the Slovenian police for a copy of his personal data and information on its processing, including the processing log (dnevnik obdelav). The police gave most of the information but refused the log entries on internal users. The Information Commissioner found a partial violation of Article 15(1) GDPR and Article 24(2) ZVOPOKD, because the controller must state the specific purposes and the dates and times of the logged processing. It ordered the police to decide the request again within 20 days and to provide the log extract with the purposes for all 366 rows. The rest of the complaint was dismissed.

After an enforcement request from residents, the Dutch DPA investigated how the municipality of Voorschoten processed household waste collection data (the 'dump history' linked to bin and token chips). It found the municipality kept this data longer than necessary, so it had no valid legal basis for it, and did not properly inform residents about the processing. The DPA imposed an administrative fine of EUR 30,000. It started from category III, moved to category II, lowered the base fine to the band minimum of EUR 120,000, and then reduced it further for proportionality because the infringements were minor. The municipality had already ended the violations by shortening retention to 14 days and informing residents again.

The EDPB issued an urgent binding decision pursuant to Article 66(2) GDPR ordering a ban on Meta Platforms Ireland’s processing of personal data collected on Meta’s products for behavioural advertising purposes on the basis of Article 6(1)(b) GDPR and Article 6(1)(f) GDPR .

The Romanian authority (ANSPDCP) investigated a homeowners' association in Hunedoara after a complaint that it had disclosed owners' names and surnames by posting them on maintenance lists without consent or another legal basis. The investigation found breaches of Article 5(1)(a) and Article 6 GDPR, for which the association received a reprimand. It was also fined in national currency for failing to act on the authority's measures, namely failing to answer its requests, which is a breach of Article 58(1) GDPR. The authority ordered the association to bring its processing into compliance and stop disclosing personal data outside cases provided by law.

A complaint was brought against a university of applied sciences (Y) that dismissed a lecturer for urgent reasons after an incident with a student. Y then sent three emails in March 2019 to students, former students and colleagues stating the dismissal followed 'fysieke agressie' (physical aggression). The Litigation Chamber found the emails were processing of personal data, that Article 6(1)(f) GDPR (legitimate interests) was not met because naming the physical aggression was not necessary, former students had no need to know, and the balancing test was failed. It issued a reprimand and no fine.

Trade unions reported that Lombardy Region had published online a regional government resolution and a share sale contract whose annexes listed personal data of about 730 employees of transport and motorway companies, including pay, litigation and in one case health data. The file was freely downloadable and indexed by search engines for a long period. The Garante found there was no legal basis for publishing the data and that the ban on disseminating health data was breached. It fined the Region EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website. No further corrective measures were ordered because the data had been removed.

A resident complained that a condominium administrator installed a two-camera video surveillance system in the building's outdoor areas without the required assembly resolution. The images could be viewed on the administrator's phone. The Garante found that the administrator, rather than the condominium, was the controller, and that the processing was unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a) and 6 GDPR. It ordered a ban on the processing (unless the condominium adopts a resolution first) and imposed a fine of EUR 1,000. The separate failure to answer an information request was archived.

The DPA fined a medical institute €7,000 for a failure to implement appropriate security measures leading to the publication of a data subject’s personal data (including health data) in response to a review she left on Google, in violation of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR.

A patient complained that a self-employed osteopath had used her detailed health data, drawn from treatment records, in a graduation thesis, and had denied doing so when asked. The Garante found that the processing was unlawful: the privacy notice lacked required elements, the controller relied on consent where it was not the right basis, the data were disclosed to the thesis supervisor and the school, and the controller was not fair in her dealings with the patient. Because the violation was treated as minor and the controller had taken corrective steps, the Garante issued a reprimand and ordered her to revise the privacy notice within 30 days, with no fine.

A local councillor complained about two articles in a daily newspaper (21 and 23 December 2021) that, with her photo, wrongly said she had been swabbed for Covid and was in isolation/quarantine. The publisher ignored her deletion requests sent the same day and did not respond to the Garante's requests or attend the hearing. The Garante found breaches of the lawfulness, fairness, minimisation and accuracy principles, the journalism rules, and the failure to respond to the data subject (Art. 12). It banned further dissemination of her data, including in the online archive, and fined the publisher EUR 20,000.
Following a request for prior consultation under Article 36 GDPR, the Italian DPA authorised a Hospital to process the health data of deceased patients in two medical studies.

A man registered in the Public Opposition Register received an unsolicited promotional call from a small Italian photovoltaic company, which had obtained the number from a US list supplier via WhatsApp. The Garante found that the company telemarketed without verified informed consent, did not check the Opposition Register, gave inadequate information in its call script and could not demonstrate accountability over its supply chain. It banned processing of data collected without valid consent, ordered deletion of such data and the adoption of verification and tracking procedures, and fined the company EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision.

The DPA fined a controller €279,100 (GBP 240,000) for making direct marketing calls to data subjects on a ‘do not call’ register, noting that controllers must verify whether data subjects are on the register and cannot rely on data suppliers' assurances.

The Slovenian Information Commissioner issued a misdemeanour decision over video surveillance carried out at premises. The notice about the surveillance was not placed at the main entrance before people entered; it appeared only later, after surveillance had already started, and surveillance was also carried out by a further camera (its label is redacted in the published text). The responsible person (a director) and the legal entity were each given a reprimand (opomin), with no fine. Each must pay a EUR 30 court fee.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in October 2023 into a car-sharing company run through a mobile app. A customer complained about marketing emails. The company could not show consent or any other legal basis for using the customer's email for direct marketing, and it kept sending marketing messages after the customer asked for erasure. The company was fined RON 4,975.20 (stated as EUR 1,000) and given a warning, and a corrective measure was imposed to ensure compliance with consent conditions.

A complainant complained to the Slovenian Information Commissioner that the controller had wrongly refused his request for access to his own personal data about his candidacy in a public tender, and had wrongly cited the secrecy of the commission's work. After the complaint, the controller sent its reply to the appeal, including the test and commission scores, and the Commissioner asked the complainant whether he still wished to pursue the complaint; he did not respond. The Commissioner found that when the complaint was lodged on 14 July 2023 the controller had not properly decided the access request, violating Article 15 GDPR in conjunction with Articles 12 and 14 of ZVOP-2. No corrective measures were ordered because the controller had subsequently provided the data, and the complainant was granted full access to the case file.

The Romanian DPA concluded an investigation into Mensajero SRL after a complaint about a possible security breach on the company's website. A link displayed a list of downloadable files, mostly invoices and warranty certificates of customers' purchases, which led to unauthorised disclosure of customers' personal data. The company had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security appropriate to the risk. It was fined 14,925.6 lei, stated to be equivalent to EUR 3,000.

The Slovenian Information Commissioner issued a misdemeanour decision under the Slovenian Personal Data Protection Act (ZVOP-2) against a company and its director. Between January and March 2023, the company ran video surveillance without the full information notice required by Article 76(4), recorded an excessive area in workplaces contrary to Article 78(2), and recorded a public road and meadow contrary to Article 80(3). For each offence the director and the company received a reprimand (opomin), and no monetary fine was imposed.

A data subject complained, through the Malta DPA, that the online casino operator Brivio Limited had not answered his access request of 22 February 2022 within one month. The controller later said the request was delayed by an internal handling failure and fully satisfied it on 12 September 2022, and it described new procedures and training. The Commissioner's preliminary decision found an infringement of Article 12(3) GDPR, and the final decision of 23 October 2023 confirmed that violation. Taking into account mitigating and aggravating factors, the Commissioner issued a reprimand and no fine.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation in September 2023 into Dante International SA, owner of the fashiondays.ro site. A complaint said the company used the complainant's phone number for direct marketing SMS messages without consent. The company could not show consent or any other legal basis, so the authority found a breach of Article 6 GDPR. It fined the company 4,974.9 (stated as equivalent to EUR 1,000) and ordered it to obtain prior express consent for marketing and to process data only on a valid legal basis.

An insurance company mistakenly e-mailed a compensation confirmation containing one customer's personal data to an unauthorised third party. It recorded the incident internally, judged the risk low and did not notify the data protection authority. The authority learned of it from the third party and opened proceedings of its own motion. It found a breach of Article 33(1) GDPR (no notification within 72 hours) and imposed a fine of PLN 103,752, about EUR 22,000. It treated the long duration, intent, a previous infringement and poor cooperation as aggravating, and found no mitigating factors for the fine.

IMY examined six complaints from Poland, Italy and the UK by people who kept receiving H&M newsletters after objecting to direct marketing. In each case H&M failed to stop the processing without undue delay, in some cases for up to about 18 months, because customer service unsubscribed people only from the general newsletter and not the customer-club newsletter. IMY found breaches of Articles 6(1), 12(2), 12(3) and 21(3) GDPR. It treated the six cases as linked processing of low seriousness, took the company's task force and technical fixes as mitigating, and imposed a fine of SEK 350,000.

A complainant alleged that her personal data in a members' list of a local section of a Belgian political party had been unlawfully used and disclosed by the party's communications manager to harm her reputation. The complaint started as a mediation request and was converted into a complaint. The Litigation Chamber found the complaint insufficiently supported by evidence and considered that investigating would not be an appropriate use of resources, especially with a judicial case already pending on the same grievances. It dismissed the complaint without examining the merits, finding no violation, and only reminded the controller of its accountability duty under Article 5(2) GDPR.

The Estonian DPA upheld a complaint filed by noyb and declared that the controller transferred personal data to the U.S. in lack of any legal basis under the GDPR. The controller was ordered to stop the processing.

The CNIL restricted committee fined a French telecoms and media company (name redacted in the text) EUR 600,000 for multiple GDPR and e-privacy breaches. The company could not prove valid consent for its electronic marketing, which relied on partner forms that did not name it, and its calls to prospects often gave incomplete or no information under Article 14. It also found that its retention information was too vague, and the operative part lists further breaches of Articles 12, 15, 28, 32 and 33. The decision orders publication of the decision, with the company's name removed after two years.

The Garante found that Scionti Selezioni Superiori S.r.l. (marketing brand Caffè Scionti) carried out unsolicited marketing calls without valid consent or information, used contact lists from third-party list providers and word-of-mouth without verifying consent, failed to properly handle data subject rights and opt-outs, did not consult the public opt-out register (RPO), and lacked accountability measures. It banned the processing of data collected without consent, ordered deletion and compliance measures, and imposed a fine of EUR 70,000.

A healthcare worker complained that colleagues had repeatedly accessed her health dossier at the Lodi hospital trust in 2019-2020, during the Covid pandemic, to find out her swab results, organise shifts and assess quality of care. The Garante found that the access was for purposes other than treatment, by staff not involved in her care, without valid consent, and that the dossier had no alert or full logging systems. It declared the processing unlawful, fined the trust EUR 40,000 and ordered it to put in place anomaly alerts and full access logging within 90 days. The decision is also published in full.

The Italian DPA issued a warning to a private person for installing a camera on the external wall of her house, which was also covering a nearby playground. The processing operation was in breach of the lawfulness and data minimisation principles.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) issued a decision on the processing of personal data by CaixaBank S.A., the controller, holding that the design of a cookie banner respected its “Guidelines on the use of cookies” of 2020.

An employee of a municipal water and sewerage company complained that her COVID-19 test result and other personal data, including health data and her social security and tax numbers, were disclosed to third parties without a legal basis. The Authority found three separate infringements of the data minimisation principle, Article 5(1)(c) GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,000 for the disclosure that took place outside the controller's sphere, and ordered the company, for the other two infringements inside its sphere, to adopt compliant internal policies on recipients of personal data and on restricted internal access to documents containing health data within three months.

Two complainants, a physician and his company, complained that two Austrian media companies had not handled their access and erasure requests after they reported on a compromised email account. The DSB found that the newspaper company and the broadcaster violated the right of access under Art. 15 GDPR by not providing several categories of information, and that the newspaper company also failed to react to the company's request. It ordered both to provide the information within four weeks. The erasure complaint and the secrecy complaint were dismissed, the latter after weighing press freedom against the complainants' interests. The Federal Administrative Court dismissed the appeals on 6 June 2024.

The Croatian data protection authority fined the debt collector EOS Matrix d.o.o. EUR 5.47 million after an anonymous complaint with a USB stick holding 181,641 individuals' data. The inspection found inadequate technical security, which meant the company could not explain how the data left its system. It also found processing of non-debtors' data without a legal basis and recording of health details, including diagnoses, without a legal basis or a valid Article 9 exception. Privacy policies wrongly said health data would not be processed, and the wording about call recording ("may be recorded") was unclear. Calls were recorded between May 2018 and January 2019 without a legal basis.

A complainant asked the website operator Technius Ltd (StripChat) for a copy of his data after someone else had opened an account using his email address. The controller asked for a government-issued ID before it would act on the request, and it told its users about a data breach only through a blog post. The Cyprus Commissioner found infringements of Article 5(1)(c) (data minimisation) and Article 34(1) (communication of a breach to data subjects) and issued a reprimand.

The Swedish DPA examined CCTV operated by the Stockholm city education board at Aspudden school, in place since 2014, for the period from 25 May 2018 to 3 October 2023. It found that the board lacked a legal basis for most of the camera surveillance during school hours, which breached the lawfulness and data minimisation principles and Article 6(1). It also found an Article 13 information breach, but imposed no fine for that. The board was fined SEK 800,000 and ordered to stop most of the surveillance and to correct the legal-basis information on its website.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in September 2023 into the energy supplier Cez Vânzare S.A., started after a personal data breach notification. The company emailed disconnection notices to natural gas customers, but some recipient addresses were typed wrongly, so the notices reached other customers. Names, postal and consumption-site addresses, and customer and site codes were disclosed. The authority found that appropriate technical and organisational security measures were missing (Art. 32(1)(b) and 32(2) GDPR) and fined the company RON 4,969.70, stated as equivalent to EUR 1,000.

A complainant received a parking charge from a Belgian municipality and, when he asked how his data was processed, learned that the municipality used an IT company without a written processor agreement. The agreement was only signed on 27 July 2020, after the facts. The Litigation Chamber found breaches of Article 28(3) by both parties, and of Articles 12(1) and 14 by the municipality, which could not rely on the exemption in Article 14(5)(c). It issued a reprimand to each defendant and ordered publication of the decision, with no fine.

A complainant wrote to the public body (called Y in the decision) about a difference in letter fonts and asked whether its correspondence templates had changed. The body treated this as a possible fraud report and opened an investigation, during which it contacted the complainant's ex-wife. The complainant later found that his name and email address had been sent to her, and he complained about this and about the answers he received. The Inspection Service found shortcomings in security documentation and in the privacy statement, and noted that these had been corrected by the time of the decision. The Litigation Chamber issued reprimands for the past infringements and the other findings were dismissed. No fine was imposed.

A German data subject complained that Airbnb required an unredacted, high-resolution copy of his identity card and a supplemental photograph to verify his identity before he could complete a booking requested by a host. The DPC, as lead supervisory authority, found that Airbnb had no valid legitimate-interests basis for this request because it made no less intrusive verification attempts first. It also found infringements of data minimisation and storage limitation for keeping the ID copies and supplemental photographs. The DPC found no infringement of the transparency or erasure rules. It imposed no fine, issued a reprimand, and ordered deletion of the supplemental photographs and a policy revision.

Datatilsynet criticised Mindworking A/S, a processor that developed and supplied a web platform used by real estate agents, for not ensuring adequate security. Users logged in could view personal data in the source code, including names and offer prices of potential buyers and, in some documents, CPR numbers, by using a function key. The flaw existed from early 2019 until 4 November 2021, and the company notified the breach in November 2021 after the authority had received reports from 65 controllers. The decision is a reprimand under Article 32(1) GDPR; no fine is imposed.

The Garante investigated Axpo Italia S.p.A., an electricity and gas supplier, after several complaints that door-to-door sales agents had concluded unrequested energy contracts using inaccurate personal data. The Garante found breaches of the principles of accuracy and fairness, and of accountability, because Axpo's controls over its agents and its CRM were inadequate. It imposed a fine of EUR 10,000,000, ordered corrective measures within nine months, and ordered a definitive restriction on processing of data of about 5,100 affected customers.

The health authority Asl Napoli 3 Sud notified the Garante of a ransomware attack on its information systems. The attackers entered through VPN using credentials of non-technical staff found on the dark web, with no multi-factor authentication, then escalated to administrator privileges and encrypted the data centres. The Garante found weak authentication and password policy, no formalised backup procedure and no recovery plan. It declared the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(f), 25 and 32 GDPR and fined the authority EUR 30,000, with publication of the decision. No corrective orders were issued because the authority had already adopted further measures.

A patient complained that, after a pulmonology sleep study, the physician emailed him the report and copied a third-party company supplying ventilation equipment, without his consent. The physician argued urgency of treatment, that the clinic held the patient's consent and that he acted as the clinic's processor. The Garante found he acted on his own, so was an autonomous controller, and had no valid legal basis for disclosing health data to a third party. It declared the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a), (c), (f) and 9 GDPR and fined him EUR 5,000, with publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered since the conduct had ceased. A note says the court challenge ended with a judgment the Garante calls 'favourable' (ordinary court, judgment 121/2025, published 26 May 2025); it does not say for which side.

The Garante fined Palombaro s.r.l., which runs a restaurant in Ancona, EUR 3,000 for operating video surveillance without information signs. A local police inspection on 22 June 2022 found the cameras working and no signage. The company said it had installed signs right after the inspection and sent photographs as proof. The Garante found breaches of Article 5(1)(a) and Article 13 GDPR and ordered publication of the decision.

The Garante received a report that medical records (prescriptions, patient files, X-rays) were lying abandoned and accessible to anyone in the disused former Banti Sanatorium owned by the Tuscany Centre health authority. The authority argued the site was guarded, the papers were old and mostly illegible, and no retention rules applied. The Garante rejected these arguments, noting that sector retention and disposal rules existed and that patient identifying data were visible in the footage. It found breaches of Article 5(1)(a), (e), (f) and Article 32 GDPR and Article 75 of the Code, imposed a fine of EUR 50,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered because the documents had been removed and disposed of.

The Ministry of Environment published on its institutional website an inspection-related annex containing names and employee numbers of workers at the Taranto steelworks (ex Ilva), including around 45 linked to health data (prescription safety glasses). The documents stayed online for 16 days and were downloaded four times. The Garante found the publication lacked a legal basis and breached the data minimisation, lawfulness and health-data rules. It imposed a fine of EUR 5,000, ordered publication of the decision, and adopted no further corrective measures since the data had been removed.

A healthcare controller charged for copies of MRI images on CD when patients asked for them without referring to Article 15 GDPR. The Deputy Ombudsman found that the controller did not charge when a patient relied on Article 15, which complies with Articles 12(5) and 15(3), but that it failed to facilitate the right of access under Article 12(2), because it did not tell patients they could get their records free of charge. The Deputy Ombudsman issued an order to bring processing into compliance and a reprimand. No fine was imposed, and the decision is final.

Following a report of a potential data security breach, ANSPDCP investigated the energy company RESTART ENERGY ONE S.A. It found that a file on the website containing personal data of at least 750 people was publicly accessible via search engine links for about two and a half years. It also found non-essential cookies were installed before consent and that refusing them had no effect. The company was fined RON 124,150 (about EUR 25,000) under the GDPR and RON 40,000 under Law 506/2004, and ordered to implement a procedure for regular testing and evaluation of its systems, especially the website.
The Croatian DPA imposed an administrative fine in the amount of €15,000 on a controller due to multiple GDPR violations in the context of its online booking system.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a self-employed person running a website. Following a complaint from a Polish citizen via IMI, the office analysed the site and found that non-technical cookies were set before any consent, and that the cookie information lacked purpose, legal basis, retention period and data subject rights. The accused was found to have breached Art. 5(1)(a) and Art. 13(1)(c) and (2)(b),(d) GDPR. A single fine of CZK 26,000 was imposed, using the absorption principle, with the two information breaches treated as aggravating. The accused was also ordered to stop cookie processing without consent, supply the missing information, fix the cookie banner and translate it into Czech.
The Spanish DPA fined €600 for installing security cameras that focused beyond the private property of the controller's, violating Article 5(1)(c) and 13 GDPR.

Following a complaint about video surveillance cameras allegedly used to monitor municipal employees, the authority investigated the Albeni commune (UAT). It found the controller had not carried out remedial measures previously ordered and had not answered the authority's requests. It also found no proof that data subjects were informed and no adequate security measures for the video system. The controller was fined 10,000 lei for the non-cooperation and given a warning for the other infringements, along with corrective orders.

The Spanish DPA fined €17,000 a local Handball Federation for requesting and processing health data of its participants in its competitions to discriminate on the basis of such data, violating Article 9 and Article 13 GDPR.

The Greek DPA carried out an on-site inspection of OASA's automatic fare collection system (the electronic ticket) in November 2019, to check compliance with its earlier opinions 1/2017 and 4/2017. The audit found that the data protection impact assessment was late and inadequate, that no retention period had been set (20 years was later chosen for all purposes without justification), and that the record of processing was incomplete. The Authority fined OASA EUR 50,000 for breach of the storage limitation principle and reprimanded it for breaching Articles 25(1) and 35(1). It also ordered OASA to define and document retention periods within one month and to revise the impact assessment within three months.

A former employee complained that his ex-employer had kept his business mailbox active after he left on 30 April 2023, and that an email was sent from his account to clients on 9 May 2023 without his consent. The Chamber dismissed the complaint about the mailbox's continued existence for lack of sufficient evidence. On the 9 May email, it found a prima facie breach of purpose limitation, data minimisation, lack of legal basis and failure to inform, and issued a reprimand. No fine was imposed, and the decision is a prima facie one that the defendant may challenge by requesting a merits hearing within 30 days.

The CNPD's restricted formation ruled on an investigation into two public bodies that had fitted service vehicles and construction machinery with GPS tracking, which could be linked to individual employees through work sheets. The investigation found that the employees were not properly informed about the tracking (Art. 13 GDPR) and that the tracking was used for a purpose that was not legitimate (purpose limitation, Art. 5(1)(b) GDPR). The authority imposed a joint administrative fine of EUR 2,500 and ordered the bodies to bring their employee information into line with Art. 13 within two months.

In one of the cookie banner mass complaints filed by noyb, the Berlin DPA found that collection of consent by the controller did not fully comply with the GDPR. However, given the improvements in the cookie banner, the DPA did not adopt any corrective measure.

The Austrian DPA ordered a controller to erase the personal data of a data subject processed upon accepting a cookie via a banner in violation of the GDPR and to inform third party providers of the erasure according to Article 17 GDPR and Article 19 GDPR.

The Austrian DPA ordered a controller to bring its cookie banner into compliance with Article 7 GDPR and to inform third party providers of the deletion of personal data of the complainant pursuant to Article 19 GDPR.

A data subject, represented by an association, complained that a US sports publisher's website set cookies with unique identifiers after a cookie banner that lacked an equal reject option, and that the publisher had not informed recipients when it deleted the identifiers. The authority upheld the complaint in part: the publisher must inform the recipients of the deletion within four weeks. The rest of the complaint was dismissed, and a further request to establish a past infringement was rejected. The authority also ordered, ex officio, changes to the cookie banner and the consent mechanism, including an equally prominent reject option and valid consent for analytics cookies.

The Romanian DPA completed an investigation in September 2023 into NN Asigurări de Viață S.A. after a complaint from a data subject who received direct marketing messages via LinkedIn. The controller ignored the person's emailed requests not to be contacted with direct marketing, breaching Article 21(3) GDPR. It was fined RON 4,946.50 (about EUR 1,000). The authority also ordered the controller to adopt appropriate internal procedures for handling data subject requests and to train staff regularly.

The French Data Protection Authority (CNIL) fined an air freight transport company EUR 200,000 for multiple GDPR infringements arising from an internal employee recruitment form for posts in China. The company collected excessive personal details regarding employees' families in violation of the data minimisation principle, and unlawfully processed special categories of data (ethnicity and political opinion) without valid consent. The company also unlawfully consulted and retained employees' criminal record excerpts (bulletin n° 3). Finally, the CNIL found a breach of the duty to cooperate under Article 31 GDPR because the company provided deliberately incomplete translations of the questionnaire and inaccurate information to investigators.

On the basis of Article 36 GDPR, the French DPA issued an opinion finding a scientific research survey project to be implemented by a data controller legitimate as its processing of sensitive personal data was necessary for scientific research purposes in the public interest.

The DPC found that Airbnb Ireland UC lawfully retained the complainant's personal data after an erasure request, as it was necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims under Article 17(3)(e) GDPR.

The Croatian DPA announced two administrative fines, of EUR 20,000 and EUR 30,000, on two gambling and betting companies. Both were found to have used cookies on their websites without a legal basis. Both also failed to let visitors give or withdraw consent separately for each type of cookie, and failed to give adequate information about the cookie processing. The press release does not name the companies or say which fine went to which.
The Croatian DPA imposed two administrative fines in the amounts of €20,000 and €30,000 on a gambling and a betting company, due to unlawful data processing via cookies on their websites.

A person reported that two SIM cards had been activated in his name without his knowledge by GFB One, a Vodafone dealer in Campania, using only a photocopy of his identity document. The Garante found Vodafone had acted lawfully but that GFB, as an independent controller, had processed the person's data without a legal basis, had given no privacy information, and had ignored the Authority's request for information. It banned GFB from any further processing of the person's data and fined it EUR 90,000. It also ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

Several employees of a cooperative complained to the Italian DPA that it had not fully answered their access requests about the data and logic used to compute their pay, mileage reimbursements and the GPS-enabled work smartphones. The company said it had already supplied the documents and that its devices only record the meter location at the time of reading. The Garante found that the company had not given a suitable reply to the access requests, in breach of Articles 12 and 15 GDPR. It ordered the company to satisfy the access requests within 60 days and imposed a fine of EUR 20,000, and ordered the decision to be published.

A doctor employed by the South Tyrol health authority, suspended for not being vaccinated against Covid-19, asked to exercise his data protection rights (access, rectification, erasure) and received no timely reply. The reply came only after the Garante intervened, well beyond the one-month limit, which the authority blamed on an internal organisational mishap. The Garante found a breach of Article 12(3) GDPR and fined the authority EUR 10,000, also ordering publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased to have effects.

An employee complained that the municipality of San Severo published on its website three determinations listing about 140 employees with name, category and the individual productivity bonus each received. The municipality admitted a wrong interpretation of the rules and a website configuration error that kept the documents online; it removed them after the Garante's inquiry. The Garante found there was no suitable legal basis for disseminating the data, since transparency law requires only aggregate, not named, publication. It fined the municipality EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

A parent complained that the bank did not answer his access request for his minor son's personal data, which had been sent to the bank's general certified email address and was lost at a branch through an operational error. The bank only replied after the Garante intervened. The Garante found a breach of Article 12(3) and (4) GDPR, declared the processing unlawful and fined the bank EUR 42,000. No injunction was issued because the information had already been supplied, and the decision is to be published.

An employee complained that his employer used a fingerprint system to record attendance without giving information or asking consent. The Garante found that the company processed biometric data of 13 employees from February 2019 to April 2022 without a valid legal basis and with an information notice that did not mention the biometric processing. It fined the company EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision. The company had replaced the system with badges during the proceedings.

The Danish Data Protection Agency examined access to patient lists in the Sundhedsplatformen system. The front page let staff with login access view patient lists across all of Region Sjælland's hospitals, including for patients they had no treatment relationship with. About 16,322 users had this access, and the logs did not show which personal data a user had actually viewed. The authority issued serious criticism (alvorlig kritik) for insufficient security under Article 32(1) GDPR.

The Spanish DPA fined BBVA €70,000 for not securely verifying the data subject's identity. A third party who had stolen the data subject's identity able to withdraw money, violating Article 6 and Article 32 GDPR.

The Office of the Data Protection Ombudsman's sanctions board fined Suomen Yritysrekisteri EUR 23,000 for failing to give complainants a proper copy of their phone call recordings. Complainants, self-employed persons, had received a sales call and asked for the recording, but the company supplied only written summaries that did not match the call. The company also ignored an earlier order from a deputy ombudsman to change its practice, and the board found the breaches intentional and wide in scope. The press release says the decision is not final and can be appealed to an administrative court.

The Spanish DPA issued a reprimand to Servicio Canario De La Salud. Medical records had been improperly accessed and the diagnosis disclosed to third parties, violating Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR.

The complainant, director of a company, asked AJPES to remove from its public Beneficial Owners Register the permanent and temporary residence addresses of her as a beneficial owner, and AJPES refused. The Information Commissioner found that AJPES had no legal basis to publish those addresses online, since the national law only provides for publication of the country of residence, and so breached Article 6(1) GDPR. By refusing the erasure request for data it had unlawfully processed, it also breached Article 17(1) GDPR. AJPES was ordered to block public access to the addresses within 40 days; no fine was imposed.

The Spanish DPA reprimanded the General Secretariat of Penitentiary Institutions of Spain for the leak of images captured by the video surveillance system of the penitentiary center of Villena (Alicante), violating Article 32 GDPR.

Following a request for prior consultation under Article 36 GDPR, the French DPA authorised the University of Bordeaux to implement automated processing of personal data for a study comparing health trajectories leading to cardio-metabolic diseases, to evaluate the interoperability of European health data.

A German data subject complained, via the German authority (Berlin SA), that her erasure request sent in January and February 2021 to a generic customer email address of the controller's German subsidiary went unanswered. The data (name and email address) were deleted in June 2021, but the controller only told her of the erasure in April 2022, after the Cyprus authority contacted it. The Commissioner found that the controller failed to notify the erasure within the Article 12(3) timeframe and lacked adequate measures under Article 24(1), and issued a reprimand rather than a fine.

Datatilsynet in Norway carried out an unannounced inspection of a candy store and ordered a ban on CCTV surveillance and transparent information to data subjects, as these were predominately employees younger than 18 years old.
The Spanish DPA fined másLUZ Energía (SIE) €70,000 for violating Article 6(1) GDPR as it unlawfully processed personal data after the cancellation of an energy and gas supply contract.

A private individual complained that the underground car parks of Y use ANPR cameras for a payment system and asked whether a data protection impact assessment had been carried out. The Dispute Chamber dismissed the complaint on the basis of a lack of personal interest. The complainant exercised no data subject rights and did not show he had used such a car park, so no effective infringement was shown and no investigation on the merits was opened. The decision says a new complaint is possible if the complainant shows personal interest and identifies the rights affected.

The Austrian data protection authority, acting on its own initiative, reviewed four video cameras operated by a public lower secondary school in corridors and the entrance area. It found that recording during school hours had no legal basis under Art. 6(1) GDPR, because a public body acting in its sovereign role cannot rely on legitimate interests and needs an explicit statutory basis, which does not exist. It ordered the school to limit the processing so that no recordings are made, or the cameras are switched off, during school operation within two weeks.
The Oslo District Court rejected Meta’s request to issue a temporary injunction against the Norwegian DPA’S earlier ban on behavioural advertisement under Article 6(1)(b) and (f) GDPR.

A complainant objected to the University of Iceland's surveillance cameras inside and outside its buildings and to the lack of signs and information about them. After a complaint, written exchanges and an on-site inspection in April 2023, the DPA found that the university's signage and information on electronic monitoring did not meet the GDPR transparency requirements. It ordered the university to fix its signs and provide the Article 13 information, and imposed an administrative fine of ISK 1,500,000, taking into account the scale of the system (97 cameras), the number of people affected and the long duration, offset by some mitigating factors.

The processing of a minor's personal data by a bank, for the purpose of a of a 'baby loan', was lawful under Article 6(1)(c) GDPR as the bank was legally obligated to collect the minor's personal data under domestic law.
The Belgian DPA ordered a controller to comply with an access request under Article 15(1) GDPR and an erasure request under Article 17(1) GDPR, after the controller failed to facilitate the requests.

After a complaint filed on 23 May 2022, the AEPD examined a fraudulent SIM card duplicate that Vodafone issued following a phone call from abroad, which let a third party access the complainant's bank account and confirm unauthorised transactions. The AEPD found Vodafone could not show it had followed its own identity-verification procedure, so the processing lacked a legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR. It proposed a fine of EUR 100,000. Vodafone paid EUR 80,000 on 20 July 2023 using one of two 20% reductions, which ended the proceedings without a further decision on the merits.

A data subject asked a psychotherapy provider several times in 2017 to 2019 for access to records of the complainant's therapy sessions under Article 15 GDPR. The controller did not answer in time, did not respond to the authority's requests for information in the stated deadline, and granted access only in April 2021. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman issued a reprimand for insufficient fulfilment of the access right, and the sanctions board imposed an administrative fine of EUR 1,600. The decision is final.

Three complainants asked Volton, an energy supplier, for copies of recorded phone calls with its staff about their contracts, and did not receive them within one month. Volton admitted the delay, blaming a surge in requests during the energy crisis, but said it later satisfied the requests. The Authority found three breaches of Article 12(3) GDPR and one breach of Article 12(2) GDPR concerning the right of access. It issued a reprimand and ordered Volton to bring its procedures into line within three months and to report back.

A lawyer complained on behalf of a ship's skipper about video footage taken by a Fiskistofa fisheries inspector, who pointed a telescope-mounted camera at the crew of a fishing vessel fishing outside the public area. Persónuvernd held that Fiskistofa had no legal basis for this processing under the law in force in March 2020, when the footage was taken, because inspections then had to be carried out in person. It also found the surveillance was in effect covert, so the transparency principle and the duty to inform were breached. No order was issued because the law has since changed.

The Spanish DPA fined a controller for providing incomplete information about the use of video cameras. Article 13 GDPR was breached since the sign contained no information about the identity of the controller nor how to exercise data subjects' rights.

The Irish DPC investigated TikTok Technology Limited's processing of personal data of child users (under 18) on the TikTok platform in 2020. The DPC found infringements of GDPR Articles 5, 12, 13, 24 and 25, including the public-by-default settings and transparency towards child users. It issued a reprimand, ordered TTL to bring its processing into compliance within three months, and imposed administrative fines totalling EUR 345 million, following a binding Article 65 decision of the EDPB.
The DPA reprimanded the City of Helsinki for making user profiles publicly searchable and visible to all through the platform's own search function when this was not necessary.

A man complained that the local bar association published court hearing notices on its website naming him and his wife as defendants in criminal proceedings, and that the notices could be found through Google. The Garante found that publishing this criminal-offence data had no legal basis under Article 10 GDPR and Article 2-octies of the Italian Privacy Code, and breached the principles in Article 5(1)(a), (c) and (f). It declared the processing unlawful and fined the bar association. A court later reduced the fine to EUR 8,000 (judgment 298/2026, provisionally enforceable); the Garante's published text shows only the reduced amount, so the original figure cannot be confirmed from it.

A patient complained that a private medical centre (a sole proprietorship) ignored his requests for access, rectification, erasure and restriction after his Covid swab report showed a wrong birth date and tax code. The report was also first emailed to a wrong, unauthorised address. The Garante found breaches of accuracy, security, lawful basis for health data and data subject rights, and fined the former owner EUR 10,000. No corrective measures were ordered since the business had been deleted from the register and the Covid emergency had ended. The decision is published in full.

A parent complained that the online newspaper Il Giorno published a photo of girls, minors who had been harassed on a train, with only their eyes pixelated, so that they could be recognised. The Garante found that the photo was excessive and not justified by information needs, breaching the journalistic rules on minors and the fairness principle in Article 5(1)(a) GDPR. It banned further processing of the image, including in the online archive, and fined the publisher EUR 25,000. It took no action on the photo's removal, since the publisher took it down, although it was briefly republished by mistake. The Court of Cassation later rejected the publisher's challenge.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a company that answered a data subject's access request of 10 February 2022 only on 16 December 2022, after two reminders from the Authority. It found a breach of the one-month deadline in Article 12(3) GDPR, with no extension notified. A fine of CZK 40,000 was imposed. The calculation followed the EDPB fining guidelines, starting from a low base because the offence was less serious, reduced as the company's turnover was unknown but it seemed small, then raised 5% for the long delay.

A woman complained that the Corriere della Sera website, run by RCS Mediagroup, published a photo of a deceased actress's handwritten will showing her name, date of birth and home address as a witness. The Garante found that publishing these identifying details went beyond what the news story needed and breached the principle of essentiality of information and lawfulness and fairness. It found the complaint well-founded on this point but unfounded on the failure to reply to her rights requests, which it excused as the request was unclear. It banned further processing of the complainant's name, birth date and address in the article and fined RCS Mediagroup EUR 10,000.

A data subject complained that an association kept his personal data and sent him a membership renewal email in August 2022, even though he had asked for erasure in October 2021 and had been told in January 2022 that his data had been deleted. The Garante found that the association had not erased the data despite the request and that no grounds prevented erasure, in breach of Article 17(1) GDPR. Because the association cooperated, had no prior violations, and had changed its procedures, the Garante treated it as a minor violation and issued a reprimand under Article 58(2)(b) instead of a fine.
The Spanish DPA fined a resident €1,500 for installing a camera in a common area, without following the mandatory legal requirements to do so, violating Article 6(1) and Article 13 GDPR.
The Spanish DPA fined €300 for installing security cameras that focused beyond the private property of the controller's, violating Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.

A complaint was lodged with the Polish DPA about a company's failure to answer a data subject's access request. In that complaint case the DPA repeatedly asked the company for explanations, and the company never supplied them, even after a phone call with its data protection officer and a promise to complete the answer. The DPA opened a separate own-initiative procedure and found that the company breached Article 31 and Article 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR by not cooperating and not giving access to the information needed. It fined the company PLN 56,592 (about EUR 12,000), treating the failure to give access as the most serious breach, with the company's two earlier reprimands and continued passivity as aggravating.

A training participant complained that a course certificate email, sent on behalf of a training provider, showed the names and national ID numbers of all participants in the visible recipient list. The Spanish AEPD opened sanctioning proceedings against ALBEN AIRPORT FACILITIES S.L for alleged breaches of Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR, proposing fines of EUR 1,500 and EUR 1,000. The company paid EUR 1,500 on 6 July 2023 using both available reductions, which acknowledged responsibility and ended the procedure; the AEPD declared the procedure terminated.
The Spanish DPA fined an individual €10,000 for publishing a video of a data subject in a vulnerable situation, without his consent, violating Article 6 (1) GDPR.

IMY received a tip that customer documents of the insurer Moderna Försäkringar (now Trygg-Hansa) could be accessed by unauthorised people. Between October 2018 and February 2021 the insurer's technical measures were inadequate, so data on about 650,000 customers, including health data and personal identity numbers, was exposed. IMY found breaches of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of SEK 35 million, set well below the cap based on the Tryg group's turnover because the breach concerned only a limited part of the business.

The Spanish DPA fined a Community €1,500 for unduly exposure of personal data to third parties that appeared in a judgement that was placed on a public bulletin board, in violation of Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR.

Following a complaint by a client, the Romanian authority found that BODY LINE SRL posted an audio-video recording of the client on the company's social media pages and used a form of address in the comments that revealed the client's ethnic origin, without a legal basis. The company also did not act on the client's erasure request, and its technical and organisational measures for the video surveillance system were found insufficient, which led to the recording being accessed and posted. The authority fined the company RON 49,322 (about EUR 10,000) and ordered corrective measures.
During an own volition inquiry into processing activities carried out by the Galway County Council, the DPC found violations of Article 5(1)(a) GDPR, Article 24 GDPR and Article 35(1) GDPR.

The Romanian authority investigated UiPath SRL after it notified a personal data breach: the data of about 600,000 users of its Academy platform was exposed on a third-party website for about 10 days because storage settings allowed unauthorised access. The authority found breaches of Articles 25 and 32 GDPR, acting as lead authority under Article 60. It fined the company RON 346,598 (EUR 70,000) and ordered it to set up a regular process for testing and evaluating the effectiveness of its security measures.

The Spanish DPA ordered a controller to reply to a data subject's request to delete personal data, to an objection of processing of data for marketing purposes, transfer to third parties and profiling

A complainant reported that a power of attorney and a payment request were first wrongly registered on a company account instead of his personal user profile, and that this happened twice. The Litigation Chamber found that the processing did not fall under any of the high-risk criteria of Article 35(3) GDPR, that the lodged complaint lacked evidence, and that the complainant had not shown he exercised GDPR rights. It dismissed the complaint on policy grounds under Article 95 §1 3° WOG, without ruling on whether an infringement occurred.

A social worker in the council's Child and Family Assessment service sent copies of an assessment report to the mother and two ex-partners without redacting sensitive personal data. The Commissioner found that the council had not implemented appropriate organisational measures to ensure security of the data, an infringement of Article 32(1) UK GDPR. The council's sign-off procedure was not robust enough, staff had little redaction training, and there had been 16 similar incidents in the previous two years. The Commissioner issued a reprimand, taking into account the council's later redaction guidance from April 2022.

After a report, the Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman examined a city's basic schools collecting bank account numbers from all pupils in advance so that scholarships could be paid quickly. Scholarships went only to some pupils, so the account numbers of those without a scholarship were collected unnecessarily. The decision found a breach of the data minimisation principle in Article 5(1)(c) GDPR, issued a reprimand, and ordered the city to bring the processing into compliance and delete the collected account numbers where there is no lawful basis.

The Croatian DPA held that a media outlet unlawfully processed personal data of a data subject as the data was not publicly available and the public interest did not prevail over the right to privacy of the data subject.

A data subject complained that a real estate agency kept sending him property-listing marketing emails after he asked several times, in June 2022, June 2022 and May 2023, to be removed from its mailing list. The Chambre Contentieuse found that his requests were objections under Article 21 GDPR and that the emails continued beyond the one-month period in Article 12(3). It issued a prima facie decision ordering the agency to comply with the objection within 30 days and to report back, with the case going to the merits if it did not comply. The agency may still ask for a merits hearing within 30 days.

Two former school staff complained that a municipal secondary school published disciplinary council reports about one of them and a pupil survey about the other on the school's Smartschool platform. The Litigation Chamber dismissed the complaint itself on technical grounds, because both publications took place and ended before the GDPR applied on 25 May 2018. Using its power to look beyond the complaint, it found infringements of the accountability principle (Art. 5(2)), the information duty (Art. 13(1)(a)), the DPO designation and registration duties (Art. 37(1)(a) and 37(7)) and the DPO tasks (Art. 39(1)). It imposed no fine and ordered the municipality to submit an action plan within three months.

The Austrian DSB examined a video surveillance system with 38 active cameras in a residential complex operated by a non-profit housing company, after an anonymous tip. It found that cameras covering entrances, lifts, stairwells and corridors, which captured all residents and visitors entering and leaving, breached the data minimisation principle. It ordered the company to restrict two package-station cameras to the parcel boxes and banned the processing by the other listed cameras, but accepted cameras covering waste, bicycle and pram rooms and the garage entrances.
The DPA held that the operator of a job application platform and recruiters making use of such a platform are not joint controllers for the processing of job applicants

The DPA reprimanded the City of Helsinki for failing to conclude a data processing agreement with the company that maintained the city's online pupil welfare service, which allowed pupils to contact a school counsellor or school psychologist.

The Belgian DPA determined that two public controllers violated several GDPR provisions for sharing personal data in order to issue a parking fine. Both controllers did not have a legal basis for such processing and did not provide adequate transparency to the data subject.

Following two complaints in 2020, the Czech DPA inspected a company running two websites. It found that from July to November 2021 the company set six third-party statistical cookies without prior consent, did not tell visitors about transfers of personal data to third countries, and transferred data (including IP addresses) to Google in the USA without meeting the transfer conditions. The Office found three offences by penalty order and imposed a single fine of CZK 89,000, calculated on the most serious offence (cookies without consent) with reductions for remedy and the unclear legal situation and increases for the other two offences.

A patient complained that, after a visit to a specialised centre of a hospital following a sexual assault, a psychologist and possibly all hospital staff could access the summary of that visit, including details of the assault. The hospital's data protection officer said access would be restricted, but no follow-up came before the complaint. The Belgian Chamber Contentieuse issued a prima facie decision finding that the hospital may have breached the GDPR's accountability and security rules (Articles 5(2), 24 and 32). It imposed a reprimand, not a fine, and said the access policy should also cover already-open files as quickly as possible.

The Norwegian SA examined a complaint by noyb, passed on by the Austrian DPA, about Telenor's use of Google Analytics on its website. Telenor had embedded Google Analytics, which processed visitors' IP addresses and cookie data, and it accepted Google's terms allowing storage and processing in the USA, with no adequate supplementary measures. The SA found that this transfer to the US infringed Chapter V GDPR, in violation of Article 44. It issued a reprimand under Article 58(2)(b) and imposed no administrative fine, finding that a ban on data flows was unnecessary because Google Analytics had been discontinued on 15 January 2021.
The Maltese DPA held that the use of personal data for a legal claim is incompatible with the household exemption under Article 2(2)(c) GDPR.

The CNPD investigated the Leudelange municipal administration, a public body, for not having appointed a data protection officer (DPO) and not having notified the DPO's contact details to the CNPD. At the start of the investigation on 9 December 2022 no DPO had been designated, despite reminders of 11 August and 23 September 2022. The restricted formation found breaches of Articles 37(1)(a) and 37(7) GDPR, took into account the municipality's later designation of a DPO, and issued a reprimand. No administrative fine was imposed, since the law excludes fines against the State and communes.

The HDPA ordered a city council in Greece to cease their processing activities, under Article 58(2) GDPR and Article 15(8) of Law 4624/2019, because of an unresolved data breach, which allowed unauthorised users to access citizens' personal data via URL manipulation.

The Maltese DPA decided that a controller, sending personal schoolwork to a data subject's personal email adress with other people in the "cc", is an infringement of Article 5(1)(f) and 32(1)(b) GDPR.

The CNIL approved a reference methodology for health data processing by organisations acting within a framework of legitimate interests. This methodology will ensure that the privacy of individuals is protected while simultaneously facilitating researchers when accessing the National Health Data System.

The CNIL has adopted two new reference methodologies to enable public bodies (MR-007) to process data from the main database of the National Health Data System(SNDS), beyond the Medicalization of Information Systems Program (PMSI). The MR-007 reference methodology governs access by organizations acting within the framework of their public interest mission to data from the main database of the National Health Data System.

A complainant asked Airbnb in July 2018 for access to his personal data and for erasure of his account. Airbnb first asked him for a copy of his ID, which he refused, and then verified him by phone call on 31 July 2018. The DPC found that requesting an ID copy breached data minimisation under Article 5(1)(c) and had no valid legal basis under Article 6(1)(f). It also found breaches of Articles 15(1), 12(1) and 12(3) in handling the access and erasure requests. No fine was imposed; the DPC issued a reprimand and ordered Airbnb to revise its internal policies and procedures on providing a cover email in English by default when a data protection rights request is received outside its privacy portal, so that people do not have to ask separately to receive communications in their preferred language.

A person who had been reported as missing asked the Slovenian Police to have media outlets delete her personal data from their online reports about her disappearance. The Police replied that it had no power over online media content. The Information Commissioner found that the Police had breached Article 17(2) GDPR at the time of the complaint, because it did not take reasonable steps to inform the media controllers of the erasure request. During the proceedings the Police notified all relevant media, so the breach was remedied and no corrective measure or fine was ordered.
The Spanish DPA fined HOLALUZ €70,000 for unlawful data processing without consent by registering the electricity supplies of several properties of the data subject, violating Article 6(1) GDPR.

The Romanian data protection authority finished an investigation at the Bucharest branch of ING Bank NV Amsterdam in June 2023. The investigation began after the bank notified a personal data breach. A PDF file containing personal data was sent without authorisation through WhatsApp, so the confidentiality of the data of a significant number of clients was lost. The authority found that the bank had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational security measures and fined it RON 14,889, equivalent to EUR 3,000.

A citizen complained about the video surveillance system near waste containers in the municipality of Modica. The municipality had hired Cat s.r.l. to supply, manage and maintain the cameras and to analyse the footage. The company acted on the municipality's behalf without a valid Article 28 agreement defining its role as processor, since its appointment as judicial police auxiliary did not meet Article 28 requirements. The Garante found processing without a lawful basis and in breach of the lawfulness principle, and fined the company EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision.

A resident reported video devices placed near waste bins. A municipality had hired a sole-trader firm to supply, run and maintain the cameras and analyse the footage. The firm processed personal data for the municipality for about six months from March 2020 without an Article 28 processor agreement; appointment as judicial police auxiliary did not meet Article 28 requirements. The Garante found processing without a lawful basis and in breach of the lawfulness principle, and fined the firm EUR 5,000, with publication of the decision.

A complaint reported a video surveillance system without information signs at a shop operated by Prodav s.r.l. in Peschiera Borromeo. A Guardia di finanza inspection on 10 November 2022 found one active camera with no notice, and no union agreement or labour inspectorate authorisation as required by Article 4 of the Workers' Statute, although staff worked in the shop. The camera was removed after the inspection. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and 13 GDPR and Article 114 of the Italian Privacy Code, and imposed a fine of EUR 1,000 and publication of the decision.

A complaint was lodged about a homeowner's CCTV cameras mounted on her building entrance, which were capable of filming the public road in both directions. An inspection by the Guardia di finanza confirmed the cameras covered public road and neighbouring addresses beyond her own property, and she did not produce documents justifying a real risk or respond to the authority's requests. The Garante found the processing unlawful under Article 5(1)(a) and Article 6 GDPR, ordered her to limit the cameras to her own property within 90 days, and imposed a fine of EUR 400.

A health trust in the Milan area notified the Garante of three data breaches: a disability-assessment summons sent to the wrong person, a Multiple Sclerosis Centre email sent to 198 patients with addresses visible in the cc field, and a lab result handed to the wrong patient, which led to a false pre-diabetes diagnosis. The Garante joined the three proceedings and rejected the trust's defence arguments. It found unlawful communication of health data in breach of Articles 5(1)(f), 9 and 32 GDPR. It imposed a single fine of EUR 12,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective orders were imposed because the conduct had ended and the trust had adopted further measures.

After a laptop containing personal data (names, dates of birth, addresses and PESEL numbers) of three people was stolen from an official car in May 2022, the UODO opened proceedings against the controller, a public body that the decision calls K. It found that the laptop was protected only by a password, not encryption, even though the controller's own earlier risk analysis had rated the loss or theft of unencrypted devices as unacceptable. The UODO found infringements of Art. 5(1)(f), 5(2), 25(1) and 32(1)-(2) GDPR and imposed a fine of PLN 15,000, citing poor cooperation and documents without verifiable dates. The decision is stated to be not final.

The Garante dealt with two complaints and several reports against the online university E-Campus. People received promotional SMS messages and calls without documented consent, and their erasure and objection requests were ignored or answered late. The privacy notice also set no clear retention period for marketing data, and the university twice failed to answer the Garante's information requests and skipped a hearing. The Garante found violations of the GDPR and the Italian Privacy Code, ordered corrective measures, banned marketing use of data without documented consent, and fined the university EUR 75,000.
The Italian DPA fined €40,000 Compara Facile s.r.l. for having performed marketing phone calls in without collecting informed consent from the data subjects.

The Italian Garante inspected the telecoms company Tiscali Italia on 3-5 May 2022 as part of its checks on marketing and profiling by telephone operators. It found that Tiscali's privacy notices gave no retention periods, and it found breaches of the principles of lawfulness, purpose limitation, data minimisation, storage limitation and accountability. It also found a breach of the transparency and accountability provisions and of Art. 130(4) of the Italian Privacy Code. Because the processing operations were linked, the Garante applied Art. 83(3) GDPR and imposed a single fine of EUR 100,000, which is 0.5% of the statutory maximum. It also ordered Tiscali to set differentiated retention periods and to build a procedure that can show the history of customers' consent changes. The decision is to be published on the Garante's website.

A resident complained that the municipality of Modica sent him fines for wrongly depositing waste, based on video recorded by cameras near waste bins, with the footage reviewed over a month later and with inadequate information signs. The Garante found that the municipality used the cameras in a non-compliant way from August 2017 to May 2021: inadequate privacy notices, excessive retention, no proper processor agreements with the camera contractors, and late appointment and publication of the data protection officer. It fined the municipality EUR 45,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.
The Italian DPA authorised a hospital to conduct medical research relating to personal data of contactable and uncontactable (deceased) data subjects.

A woman complained that she kept receiving promotional calls on behalf of Maximum International Corp. S.r.l. without consent, even after objecting, and that her access and erasure requests went unanswered. The company denied being the controller, saying independent agencies sell its products. The Garante held Maximum to be the controller and found failures of accountability, of data subject rights handling, of consent for the calls, and of consent on its website form, where marketing and profiling consent was mandatory. It banned processing of website data without valid consent, ordered erasure and corrective measures, and fined the company EUR 5,000, with publication of the decision.
The Spanish DPA fined a company €10,000 for recording and publishing images of minors on its social media without having the consent of their parents.

A taxpayer complained that the Belgian city's tourist-tax form asked property owners for the name, date of birth and stay dates of every occupant, including people not registered at the property, which he considered excessive. The Litigation Chamber issued a warning, prima facie, because the data collection appeared to lack a legal basis and to breach the minimisation principle. It also reminded the city that its data protection officer also acts as archivist, which may raise a conflict of interest, and noted that the data should be erased if unlawfully collected. The decision is not a ruling on the merits; the city may request a merits review within 30 days.

The EDPS found, after the CJEU requested for an authorisation of contractual clauses under Article 48(3)(a) of the EU GDPR, that no data transfers took place that would fall under the scope of such authorisation in the context of the CJEU’s use of the videoconferencing tool Cisco Webex.

The Athens Medical Association (AMA) collected its members' Covid-19 vaccination certificates to comply with domestic public health legislation. The Hellenic DPA (HDPA) held that the processing carried out by was lawful for the purposes of Article 6(1)(e) GDPR.
The DPA imposed a fine of €48,000 on a energy company for failing to provide access to information required by the DPA as part of its investigative powers granted under Article 58(1) GDPR.
